newsitem.title: USA: Albright to visit Middle East, urges speedier talks.
newsitem.headline: Albright to visit Middle East, urges speedier talks.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday she planned to go the Middle East at the end of August and would try to bring forward talks on the shape of a final Israeli-Palestinian peace settlement.

But she said her trip depended on an improved security situation, and President Bill Clinton warned the peace process could not go on unless the Palestinians halted "terrorist" acts like last Wednesday's Jerusalem bombing.
"The Palestinian commitment to fight terror must be constant and absolute. This is essential to move the peace process forward," Albright said at the National Press Club.

Clinton told a White House news conference that until Israelis are convinced President Yasser Arafat and the Palestinian Authority is "making 100 percent effort on security, it is impossible for peace to proceed."
"If we can resolve that, then the secretary of state will soon go to the Middle East with the ideas that we have developed for going forward," he added.
After the bombing, Israel moved to punish Palestinians, withholding millions of dollars owed their Authority.

Albright, in a telephone call on Wednesday, discussed with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a process whereby Israel would resume the funding if Palestinians shared intelligence with Israel and arrested extremists, U.S. officials said.
But House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich urged Clinton to tell Arafat U.S. aid will also end unless he takes "all steps needed" to find and punish those behind acts of political violence.
U.S. mediator Dennis Ross will discuss ways of improving the security situation in a visit to the region this weekend.

"We now face a crisis of confidence that has put at risk past gains and rekindled old animosities," Albright said, adding that restoration of a sense of security was essential if the peace process was to be rebuilt.
Clinton, along with Albright, also criticised Israel for taking unilateral steps, including building Jewish settlements on traditionally Arab land, that enraged the Palestinians.

"We've made it clear to the Israelis that we don't think anything should be done which undermines the trust of the parties and violates either the spirit or the letter of the Oslo accord, and which predetermines the outcome of final settlement issues under Oslo," Clinton said.
Albright declined to give details of her planned trip.

"I will consult closely with the leaders of the region and especially with Israeli and Palestinian leaders to improve the climate for negotiations and to discuss the procedural and substantive aspects of the permanent status issues," she said.
She said the U.S. favoured "accelerating permanent status negotiations. Today this step is urgent and important."
Netanyahu has already proposed rapid "final status" negotiations between Israel and the Palestinians to wind up in six months, instead of the original 1999 deadline.
U.S. officials said Arafat also favours a speedier process but differences remain between the two sides on what must happen before that accelerated process can begin.
Final status talks are meant to settle the borders and nature of the Palestinian entity -- Palestinians want an independent state -- and the administration of Jerusalem.

In a clear message to Arafat, she said: "The terrorists are unrelenting and so we must be unrelenting in our struggle against them. On this issue, there can be no winks, no double standards, no double meanings and with respect to the imprisonment of terrorists, no revolving doors."
Albright stressed Washington would not become a party to the talks but would be there at the table. "Only the parties can make the decisions but we will support them," she said.

Albright has been in contact with the leaders in the region by telephone and during their visits to Washington but has resisted travelling to the Middle East herself until she felt sure concrete progress could be made.
The Clinton administration -- and Albright specifically -- have come under pressure to intervene actively after talks between Israelis and Palestinians broke down six months ago.
